subject: physics
title: Force
summary: A force is a push or a pull — the thing that starts, stops, or turns a pickup — like your foot to a ball (a 20 N kick). Forces are vectors drawn as arrows. Balance the arrows and nothing changes; tip the balance and the object accelerates. Explore how tiny pushes and giant pulls both read in newtons (N).

compareCandidate.label: Force vs. momentum

plainLanguageExplanation: A force is just a push or a pull — the simplest idea in physics. Your hand pushes a door (push), a magnet pulls a pin (pull), gravity pulls everything down (pull). Every force has a size, measured in newtons (N), and a direction; so a force is a vector — you draw it as an arrow, long for big forces, pointing the way it acts. The trick that matters most is balance: if every force on an object cancels, the net force is zero and the object keeps doing what it's doing (rest or steady motion). The moment the forces don't cancel — like a tug-of-war one side pulls harder — a net force shows up, and only then does the object accelerate. In the model you tug on a box with two forces at once and watch the arrow algebra: two 10 N pushes on opposite sides come to 0 N net; two pulls the same way sum to 20 N. Everything about force — the unit, the arrows, the balance — is ready for Newton's second law (F = ma) right afterward.

keyFacts.label: Definition
keyFacts.value: A push or a pull acting on an object

keyFacts.label: Vector
keyFacts.value: Has a size AND a direction; drawn as an arrow

keyFacts.label: Balanced forces
keyFacts.value: They cancel to zero net force — no change in motion

keyFacts.label: Unbalanced forces
keyFacts.value: A leftover net force — the object accelerates

whyItMatters: Force is the everyday word full of physics: catching a ball uses a force, a rocket needs forces, and every machine — from a bicycle to a crane — is designed around pushes and pulls measured in newtons. Balancing forces is how engineers keep a bridge standing and how a feather and a brick hit the ground together when air is removed. Understanding forces unlocks the rest of mechanics (acceleration, momentum) and even chemistry; it is the single concept most present in your daily life.
didYouKnow: The newton is the force that gives a 1 kilogram mass an acceleration of 1 m/s². So when you hold a 1-liter bottle of water still, you're pushing up with about 9.8 N — the same as the force of gravity on it.
compareReason: A force is a push/pull applied now; momentum stores the motion an object already has. Watching a box build momentum as a constant net force acts shows how they're related.
